author: Furetière / Basnage de Beauval
phrase: On compte 8. Croisades.
notes: Count reported as custom; no reason given.

author: Ephraim Chambers
phrase: They reckon eight Croisades for the Conquest of the Holy Land
notes: Translates the French formula.

author: C.-G. Koch
expeditions_affected: H6 dropped; D and F split; Tunis not numbered
phrase: On en compte proprement sept
notes: 'Proprement' implies a correction of the current eight (Moréri's), not a report of custom. No reason given for the slots.

work: Tableau sommaire du cours d'histoire générale
author: Desmichels and Trognon
phrase: Expédition d'André, roi de Hongrie, 1217. Cinquième croisade [1228]
notes: Exclusion by layout: Andrew's expedition is listed without a number.

work: Tableau chronologique de l'histoire du moyen âge
author: Desmichels
expeditions_affected: D numbered fifth; Tunis numbered eighth
phrase: Huitième et dernière croisade. [1270]
notes: The switch from r04 is made without comment.

author: Courtin
phrase: On compte communément huit croisades

author: Lévi Alvarès
phrase: (paraphrase) refuses to count Frederick II's voyage as a crusade
notes: Exact wording not re-read in this pass. The only explicit argument against a slot found before 1842.

work: Dictionnaire universel d'histoire et de géographie
author: Bouillet
phrase: On compte généralement huit croisades.

author: (Landois et al.)
phrase: Nous avons suivi l'usage le plus général
notes: First statement of custom about slots rather than the total.

author: Pierer
phrase: gewöhnlich gar nicht gerechnet
notes: The 1202-04 expedition 'usually not counted at all'. Reason implied: it never reached the Holy Land.

author: Larousse
phrase: on donne plus généralement le nom de quatrième croisade à celle ... du roi de Hongrie
notes: Custom invoked for a different slot assignment.

author: G. W. Cox
phrase: This expedition may be regarded as the seventh in the list
notes: Barons' Crusade admitted as a numbered slot.

author: P. V. N. Myers
phrase: (footnote) counting Henry VI's expedition 'the number increased to nine'

author: Gilman et al.
phrase: the first four Crusades are the only ones to which the same numbers are assigned by unanimous consent
notes: Also 1917.

author: Louis Bréhier
phrase: This division is arbitrary and excludes many important expeditions
notes: Uses the eight while calling it arbitrary.

phrase: Though conventionally the crusades are numbered, their distinctness cannot be maintained

author: ed. Edward Eyre
phrase: The conventional numbering of the Crusades has, for the sake of convenience, been [kept]
While the Crusades are numbered, they should be considered as one great [movement]
notes: School reader.

work: An Outline History of the Church by Centuries
author: Joseph McSorley
phrase: The numbering of the Crusades is arbitrary—a conventional highlighting
notes: Also 1948-49 eds.

author: Régine Pernoud
phrase: The customary numbering of the Crusades has been followed

author: Hans Eberhard Mayer
phrase: somewhat dubious ... numbering of the crusades lacks all consistency
notes: German original 1965. Text continues 'Many scholars do ...' (cut off).

author: D. H. Green
phrase: the conventional numbering of the crusades
The numbering of these crusades is conventional for the movement was essentially continuous
The numbering of the Crusades as here presented has become traditional
notes: Also 1973 and 1979.

work: A History of Christianity in Asia
author: Samuel H. Moffett
phrase: The numbering of the crusades varies, but for convenience

author: Jeffrey Burton Russell
phrase: The conventional numbering of the Crusades is not particularly helpful

work: The Crusades from the Perspective of Byzantium and the Muslim World
author: Laiou and Mottahedeh (eds.); chapter probably by Giles Constable, verify
phrase: numbering of the crusades, which differs widely both in the sources and in [modern works]
notes: Quotes Mayer in the same passage.

work: Manuel des aspirants au baccalauréat ès-lettres
author: Bouchitté, Charma, Saigey, Lesieur
phrase: Nous avons adopté la division des croisades indiquée dans le Précis d'histoire du moyen-âge de M. Desmichels.
source: D1 pass 2026-11-28 (Google Books -Tej2l1vxU4C, p. 158, image viewed)
notes: Earliest explicit attribution of the modern eight to a source. New kind 'attribution' (proposed).

author: Ernest Barker
phrase: Crusades appear to have been dignified by numbers when they followed some crushing disaster - the loss of Edessa in 1144, or the fall of Jerusalem in 1187 - and were led by kings and emperors; or when, like the Fourth and Fifth Crusades, they achieved some conspicuous success or failure.
notes: Same footnote names the crusades of 1101, 1123-24, Henry the Lion 1172 and Edward I 1271-72 as 'not reckoned in the usual numbering'. Kept in EB14 (1929), moved into the text. Echoes Procter (r31).

author: George Procter
target: H6 as fourth; count of nine
phrase: some writers have dignified the abortive result with the title of the Fourth Crusade; and numbered the subsequent expedition, which was directed against the Byzantine Empire, as the Fifth of Nine.
notes: Footnote to the German expedition of 1195-97.

author: George Procter
phrase: the more usual, which seems also the more convenient division, restricts the term of distinct Crusades to Seven, or at most Eight, great efforts, which were either produced by some signal occasion, such as the loss of Edessa or Jerusalem, or else productive of some considerable event.
notes: Also a statement of custom (seven or eight). Barker 1911 (r29) gives the same two criteria.

author: W. B. Stevenson
phrase: The crusades have been numbered as if they were a series well-defined and easily counted. Some eight ... have been selected as "the eight crusades." They are chosen on no clear principle.
notes: Continues: 'Only the first crusade is rightly defined by the numeral attached.' Uses the numbers only in quotation marks.

work: The History of England during the Middle Ages
author: Sharon Turner
phrase: He died before Tunis, in what is called the seventh Crusade, in 1270.
notes: Gibbon's L2 7 reported as usage.

author: Samuel G. Goodrich
notes: OCR; the dates read 1096, 1101?, 1147, 1189, 1195, 1202, 1217, 1228, 1240, 1248. Goodrich's own count is Gibbon's seven. Compare the Americana chronological table (sd2-1831-americana-chron-table).

author: H. Le M. Chepmell
phrase: The Crusade of the Germans (or the Fourth Crusade) ... The Fourth (or Fifth) Crusade ... The Fifth (or Sixth) Crusade ... The Seventh (or Ninth) Crusade
notes: Gibbon's seven with the nine-count in parentheses.

author: Ephraim Emerton
phrase: The phrase "fifth crusade" includes the long series of expeditions and negotiations that went on between the years 1217 and 1230.
notes: Also 'the so-called sixth crusade' for Louis IX's two crusades.

author: O. J. Thatcher and F. Schwill
phrase: The expedition which is called the fourth crusade (1202-1204) did not proceed against the Mohammedans
notes: Follows an unnumbered account of Henry VI's crusade.

author: T. F. Tout
phrase: Started in 1217 for what is generally called the Fifth Crusade.
This is sometimes spoken of as the Fifth Crusade. What is more usually called the Fifth Crusade was led by Frederick II of Germany
notes: Of the Damietta crusade. Same sentence in 1924 and 1953 (sd-1953-americana).

work: Mosheim, Institutes of Ecclesiastical History (Murdock tr.)
author: James Seaton Reid (editor's note)
phrase: This is reckoned the sixth crusade by all authorities
notes: Signed 'R.'; the anchor is unclear in the OCR (Louis IX's crusade of 1248 or of 1270).

author: W. H. Davenport Adams
phrase: This is included in the Fifth Crusade by some authorities; and the Seventh Crusade is then known as the Sixth. Others reckon as the Fourth Crusade that which was undertaken by the Emperor Henry VI.
notes: Footnote to 'The Sixth Crusade, 1240-1241' (Richard of Cornwall). The table also gives 'The Fifth (or Sixth) Crusade 1216-1220'.
